items.title: [reuters.com] Russia's independent Novaya Gazeta to close Nov. 9 under pressure
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

Novaya Gazeta, one of Russia’s last independent newspapers still operating inside the country, says it will end operations on Nov. 9 after losing access to its Moscow office and reader-donation system. Editor-in-chief Sergei Sokolov said Russian authorities and security services had forced the newsroom to stop working. The paper plans to publish a final issue. The closure follows years of restrictions that intensified after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Authorities revoked the paper’s media licence, blocked its website and designated it a “foreign agent” in September 2026. This month, police searched Sokolov’s home, and investigative reporter Oleg Roldugin was arrested in a criminal case. Novaya Gazeta says the loss of its premises and funding left it unable to continue. Its separately operated sister publication, Novaya Gazeta Europe, will keep publishing from abroad. Founded in 1993, the newspaper became known for investigations into corruption and human-rights abuses. Six of its journalists and contributors were killed, including Anna Politkovskaya, who reported on the Chechen wars.

Bavaria’s government says it will restore the fire-gutted Eagle’s Nest, the former Nazi retreat in the Bavarian Alps, after officials warned the structure may not be salvageable. The blaze left the Kehlsteinhaus almost completely destroyed. Crews extinguished the last flames on Saturday but had not entered the building because of concerns it could collapse. Police are investigating a 33-year-old German man detained near the scene as firefighters and police drove up the mountain. Prosecutors said a psychiatric assessment found signs of possible mental illness and that investigators were also examining a possible political motive. Police said there was no current indication of other suspects. Bavarian Interior Minister Joachim Herrmann said the site would not be left in ruins. Officials have yet to decide what restoration will involve. Herrmann said they would discuss the next steps with local officials, historians and preservationists, and stressed the importance of continuing historical remembrance.

items.title: [Fast Company] Could AI give older creatives a second act?
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

Advertising is made for the young by the young. 

That’s conventional wisdom backed up by the Bureau of Labor Statistics, which in 2025 reported the median age of ad industry workers was 39, compared to 42 for the broader workforce. Meanwhile, a report from the World Advertising Research Center estimates that only 5% to 10% of budgets are directed toward older consumers.

Today, brands focus on Gen Z customers and ad companies target Gen Z hires, all on newer platforms like TikTok. As the new guard sweeps in, the people who built the previous era creep toward irrelevance. As AI is impacting every aspect of the industry, it’s only natural to assume that it, too, will usher in a new era of ad makers and consumers. 

It doesn’t have to. Some of the most compelling artists who incorporate AI I encounter are not necessarily very young workers coming straight out of school. They are older, established game designers, VFX artists, concept artists, animators, photographers, and directors who have spent decades devising concepts and developing characters, images, and entire imaginary worlds that have earned fandoms.  

These professionals have played with light, composition, performance, movement, texture, and narrative. They know how to make the moment big and cinematic and, more importantly, they pick up on when it feels wrong.

AI can generate campaigns, but it cannot replicate genuine experience. And if these experienced workers can leverage the technology, it could, potentially, revitalize their careers.

The Last Generation of Analog Talent

The common assumption is that AI belongs to digital natives. But knowing how to run a new model is not the same as knowing what to create with it. 

Those who came up in the analog era can immediately discern when an image lacks tension or a lens choice feels off. They know when a character could go viral and move them to the front of the scene. That’s judgment that comes with experience, not with AI.

Great things happen when proven talents are unleashed in new areas: Think of editors generating the images they once had to search for, or a game designer taking their vision to directing a commercial shoot. 

It’s understandable, though, that agencies recruit youth for AI. After all, the algorithm on career sites seeks AI talent based on specific tool fluency, and doesn’t delve into broader AI exposure and career experience.

But those who are looking find a technologically attuned older workforce. A new report by job training nonprofit CWI Works and IPSOS found that 90% of people 55 and older who have used AI for work were somewhat comfortable with AI, and 50% were extremely comfortable using it. Among Gen X respondents, 71% have used generative AI, tracking right alongside the 74% of millennials. 

This is not a closed-minded cohort. Just because someone isn’t a 22-year-old grad doesn’t mean they’re not curious about this tool. That curiosity, combined with decades of experience, is a powerful thing.

Prompting is not the profession

AI skills matter, but new tools expire quickly. Today’s specialization is tomorrow’s button click. Taste, however, can never become a button.

I have worked as a copywriter and creative director at agencies for a decade. When I started Dolsten & Co. 18 months ago as an AI-first creative agency and production company, I was building something new but was inspired by the stellar talent I’d learned from through my career. 

In recent months, Dolsten & Co. brought in an experienced copywriter, game designer, and storyboard artist with decades of experience to work on board. The copywriter built an immersive digital experience for us, while we enlisted the game designer to build a world for a TV commercial, and the storyboard artist shaped a beautiful narrative for a brand film. Their careers had been displaced by industry upheaval and hiring biases—consolidations, cost cutting, and a push for offices to “look” younger—but talent remains, and the three are shaping brand narratives and AI-driven content for leading brands using their rich experience. 

I knew that the AI skills would come, and that they’d enable these kinds of valuable, second-act experts to bring incredible ideas to life. Our hiring philosophy has brought incredibly diverse talent.

Experience is never obsolete

Advertising is notoriously dismissive of older creative talent. Experience is expensive, and senior people are pushed toward smaller management pools. Specialists can find their craft devalued when the industry adopts a different production model. 

These are valid reasons for the talent drain, but AI creates the possibility of a different trajectory. This doesn’t mean younger creators are less important. The most interesting teams combine youth’s speed, experimentation, and cultural fluency with the judgment and discipline of experienced artists.

AI will continue to automate certain tasks and compress workflows. As the creative industry dwells on what AI is replacing, the more provocative question is who it will allow to begin again.

items.title: [cbc.ca] Canadian police suspend use of Crime Stoppers after 1.5 million records exposed
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

Canadian police services are suspending their use of Crime Stoppers after a breach exposed more than 1.5 million tips submitted across Canada over 25 years, a CBC News investigation found. More than 850,000 records included personally identifiable information. The tips were managed through P3, software provided by U.S.-based Navigate360. Navigate360 acknowledged on Friday that its database had been breached between November 2025 and March 2026 and said potentially exposed information included names, addresses, birth dates and Social Security numbers. The company said it had no evidence the information had been used for fraud or identity theft. Police in several provinces have paused their use of the service while they assess the breach and its safeguards. Toronto and Ottawa police are directing people to report information through police channels, which do not necessarily offer the same anonymity. Crime Stoppers chapters and police are seeking further details from Navigate360. The company said it hired a cybersecurity firm to help strengthen security.

items.title: [nasa.gov] 4.1-billion-year-old Mars meteorite reveals evidence of ancient water
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

NASA-funded researchers say Teghaza 001, a meteorite found in Mali’s Sahara in 2022, formed in Mars’ crust at least 4.1 billion years ago, potentially making it the oldest of about 435 Martian meteorites identified on Earth. The study, published in Science on Oct. 29, describes a rare sample from the planet’s early crust; only three known Martian meteorites date to that period. The rock is a coarse-grained igneous material called gabbro, formed as magma cooled underground. Its oxygen and hydrogen isotope signatures, along with altered minerals, indicate that water reached deep into the crust and interacted with rock more than 4.1 billion years ago; the rock itself likely formed earlier. Spacecraft observations have also shown evidence of ancient water on Mars. Researchers say the evidence supports the possibility that early Mars had habitable conditions, but does not show that life existed there. Orbital mineral data point to 13 possible source locations in the planet’s southern highlands, but the meteorite’s precise birthplace remains unknown.

items.title: [abcnews.com] Swift telescope shutdown ends rapid alerts for cosmic explosions
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

NASA shut down its Swift Observatory in late October after it could no longer hold steady enough for observations, ending a 22-year mission to detect gamma-ray bursts, supernovas and other high-energy events. Swift’s rapid observations helped direct other space telescopes toward eruptions for more detailed study, and astronomers are working out how to replace that alert function. The observatory resumed observations after the rescue effort ended and captured additional gamma-ray bursts and other ultrahigh-energy events before NASA turned off its systems. Over its mission, Swift recorded more than 2,000 gamma-ray bursts and 1,400 exploding stars.

items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

Canada’s first youth-led federal climate trial opened Oct. 26 in Vancouver, where 15 plaintiffs argue the federal Net-Zero Emissions Accountability Act and the 2030 plan fail to cut emissions enough to protect their health and safety. The plaintiffs cite personal harm from heat, wildfire smoke and extreme weather. Canada has warmed about twice as fast as the global average since 1970 and could warm 5 C by century’s end under current global policies, according to federal climate assessments cited in Canadian reporting. Plaintiffs describe smoke-related illness, displacement, flooding and drought. The federal government says Canada cannot guarantee a safe climate on its own, disputes a constitutional duty to do so and argues climate change requires a global response. Witnesses are expected to testify over four to five weeks; closing arguments are scheduled for February 2027, with a decision expected later that year.

items.title: [cw39.com] Researchers favor permanent standard time as US debates clock changes
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

Most U.S. clocks turn back one hour Nov. 1, as new research reviews renew debate over whether year-round standard time or daylight saving time better supports health. A Canadian policy analysis and a review focused on people with mental illness argue that permanent standard time better protects sleep, mood and biological rhythms. A broader review of population studies, however, finds a mix of harms and benefits from seasonal clock changes and summer daylight saving time. Permanent daylight saving time would delay winter sunrise, while permanent standard time would bring earlier summer sunrises and winter sunsets. The U.S. House passed a bill to make daylight saving time permanent in July 2026, but the Senate has not taken it up. The next seasonal clock change is scheduled for March 14, 2027.

items.title: [japantoday.com] Serbia’s student-backed list projected to win majority as Vučić concedes defeat
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

The student-backed Student List is projected to win a majority in Serbia’s parliament after former President Aleksandar Vučić conceded defeat in Sunday’s snap election, ending his Serbian Progressive Party’s 14-year dominance. Vučić said the list could take 135 to 140 of the 250 seats, against about 105 for his party; separate pollster projections put the Student List at 138 seats. The count remained preliminary. Turnout reached 67.6% by 7 p.m., the highest since Yugoslavia’s breakup in 1992. The election followed nearly two years of protests sparked by the November 2024 collapse of a railway-station canopy in Novi Sad that killed 16 people. Protesters blamed corruption and failures of oversight, accusations the government rejected. The movement’s anti-corruption campaign drew support beyond students, and it entered the election with a slate of civil society candidates. With final results still pending, the Student List faces the task of forming a government without a single established leader. Its candidates have limited political experience. European Union officials offered help with rule-of-law and media reforms, while Vučić alleged foreign interference without providing evidence.
